extraction.name: FLEURS: Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech
extraction.description: An n-way parallel speech dataset in 102 languages built on top of the machine translation FLoRes-101 benchmark, with approximately 12 hours of speech supervision per language. FLEURS can be used for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Speech Language Identification (Speech LangID), Translation and Retrieval.
extraction.creator: Alexis Conneau, Min Ma, Simran Khanuja, Yu Zhang, Vera Axelrod, Siddharth Dalmia, Jason Riesa, Clara Rivera, Ankur Bapna
extraction.citeAs: Conneau, Alexis; Ma, Min; Khanuja, Simran; Zhang, Yu; Axelrod, Vera; Dalmia, Siddharth; Riesa, Jason; Rivera, Clara; Bapna, Ankur. FLEURS: Few-shot Learning Evaluation of Universal Representations of Speech. arXiv:2205.12446v1, 2022.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset is built on top of the FLoRes-101 dataset. The authors used the dev and devtest sets of FLoRes-101, containing 2009 sentences total, and split them into new train, dev, and test splits with 1509, 150, and 350 sentences respectively. For each sentence in 102 languages, they collected three recordings by three different native speakers, imposing a sex ratio balance of at least 30/70% when possible. After recording, each recording was evaluated by additional workers to assess whether it corresponded to the input sentence, and invalid recordings were discarded. The collected data was then split into train, development, and test sets with disjoint speakers between train/dev and test, with a target ratio of 7:1:2. All segments are within 30 seconds and sampled at 16kHz.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: In the first version of the dataset, about 21.5% of the sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated, leaving between zero and three recordings per sentence in the final dataset.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: FLoRes-101 contains 3001 sentences extracted from English Wikipedia and translated into 101 languages by human translators. FLEURS uses the dev and devtest sets of FLoRes-101 and collects spoken recordings of those sentences from native speakers. Source transcripts are reused from the human translators' transcripts from FLoRes-101, and English translated transcripts are also maintained.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors split the 2009 selected FLoRes sentences into new train, dev, and test splits with 1509, 150, and 350 sentences respectively. They discarded invalid recordings after worker validation and then split the collected data into train, development, and test sets with disjoint speakers between train/dev and test, targeting a 7:1:2 ratio.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All recordings are kept as they are, either from quiet or noisy environment, without data augmentations such as SpecAugment, speed perturbation, or simulated reverberation. The speech sampling rate is 16kHz. For text, the dataset provides tokenized versions of sentences. The authors apply NFC and then FST normalization to each sentence, lower-case, normalize and remove punctuations. They also split words into characters and define word boundaries. For each sentence, three versions are provided: the original raw transcript (SRC RAW), the preprocessed version (SRC NORM), and the character-based version (SRC CHAR), which should be used for ASR.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For each sentence, three recordings were collected from three different native speakers. After recording, each recording was evaluated by additional workers to assess whether the recording corresponds to the input sentence. Invalid recordings were discarded. The dataset also reuses transcripts produced by human translators from FLoRes-101.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Recordings were validated by additional workers, and invalid recordings were discarded, leaving between zero and three recordings per sentence in the final dataset.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Three recordings per sentence by three different native speakers; each recording additionally evaluated by additional workers
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Native speakers; balance in terms of sex ratio of at least 30/70%, when possible
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is publicly available via TFDS and Huggingface. In the first version, about 21.5% of sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated, and the authors state they plan to fill these gaps in future versions of the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The goal of FLEURS is to enable speech technology in more languages and catalyze research in low-resource speech understanding. The authors hope the dataset will catalyze research in few-shot understanding in many languages, enabling progress towards building speech technologies for everyone.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that results are much better on Western European languages than on groups like Sub-Saharan African or South Asian, which can be explained in part by larger amounts of unlabeled data in Western European languages from pre-training corpora. The authors also note degradation for groups known for mixing textual systems, and that CJK languages are difficult due to many homophones. They further note issues such as Urdu utterances being transliterated into Devanagari script and tokenization mismatch affecting retrieval performance on CJK languages.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Because the test set of FLoRes-101 is not publicly available, only the dev and devtest sets were used. In the first version, about 21.5% of sentences are missing because none of the three recordings were validated. Training a giant model from scratch on FLEURS will easily overfit. The paper reports poorer performance for unseen languages due to limited supervised data, poorer performance for some geographical groups with limited publicly available pre-training data, difficulties for CJK languages due to homophones, and tokenization mismatch issues in retrieval. The authors also note that avoiding over-fitting on speaker ID is essential for the LangID task.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: FLEURS can be used for Automatic Speech Recognition, Speech Language Identification, Translation, Retrieval, Speech-to-Text and Speech-to-Speech Translation, and multilingual Speech-to-Speech and Speech-to-Text Retrieval. The paper uses it as a benchmark for evaluation and provides train, development, and test splits. The character-based transcript version (SRC CHAR) should be used for ASR.
